neolithic-revolution.summary: Independent domestication of plants and animals in the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes and elsewhere, ending the exclusively foraging way of life.

sahul-separation.summary: Post-glacial sea-level rise flooded the land bridges, separating Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania and isolating their peoples from one another for the next eight thousand years.

holocene.summary: The current interglacial epoch. Every agricultural society, city and written record belongs to it.

kuk-swamp-agriculture.summary: Drainage ditches at Kuk Swamp show banana, taro and yam cultivation from around 7000 BCE — one of only a handful of places worldwide where farming was invented rather than adopted from elsewhere.

malaria.summary: Endemic across the tropics for millennia, shaping human genetics through traits like sickle-cell that confer partial resistance at a cost.

potato-domestication.summary: Domesticated around Lake Titicaca and bred into thousands of varieties suited to different altitudes. After 1492 it became a staple of Europe and, in Ireland, the subject of a catastrophic dependence.

maize-domestication.summary: Bred from a grass called teosinte in the Balsas valley over millennia of selection, maize became the staple that every later Mesoamerican civilisation was built on. One of a handful of independent inventions of farming worldwide.

tuberculosis.summary: Has probably killed more people than any other infectious disease in history, and still kills over a million a year despite being curable.
tuberculosis.note: Found in Neolithic remains; the deep start reflects the earliest skeletal evidence, not a discrete outbreak.

horse-domestication.summary: Riding turned the steppe from a barrier into a highway and gave its peoples a military advantage over settled neighbours that lasted until gunpowder.
horse-domestication.note: The Botai culture of northern Kazakhstan shows the earliest strong evidence, around 3500 BCE, but genetic work suggests modern domestic horses descend from a later lineage on the Pontic-Caspian steppe.

norte-chico.summary: The oldest known complex society in the Americas, raising monumental platform mounds on the Peruvian coast while the pyramids were being built in Egypt — and apparently without pottery or warfare.

cuneiform.summary: Sumerian accountants in Uruk turned clay tokens into impressed signs, producing the earliest known writing system and the beginning of recorded history.
cuneiform.significance: Recorded history begins here, and it begins with accounting. The earliest writing is not poetry or scripture but a record of who owed what grain to whom.

bronze-age.summary: The era of tin-bronze metallurgy, palace economies and the first long-distance trade networks across Eurasia.

indus-valley.summary: The largest Bronze Age civilisation by area, with planned cities at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, standardised weights, and a script that remains undeciphered.
indus-valley.significance: Larger in area than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, with standardised weights and planned drainage - and a script nobody can read. It is the largest early civilisation we understand the least.
